opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my default is to bet on the general model. Again and again we've seen that when you train one big model on a broad mix of data, the capabilities reinforce each other. Coding helps reasoning, reasoning helps math, multilingual data helps everything a bit. You get transfer you didn't plan for. If you split things up too early, you give that away, and you end up maintaining a zoo of models that each know a slice of the world.

That said, "one model" doesn't have to mean every parameter fires on every token. That's a lot of why I've been excited about mixture-of-experts style approaches: you can have specialization *inside* a single model. The network learns which parts to route to for which inputs, instead of a human deciding upfront that this is the legal model and that's the medical model. Let gradient descent figure out the boundaries. It's usually better at it than we are.

Where I'd split things out is mostly practical, not philosophical. One case is latency and cost. If you've got a narrow, extremely high-volume task, a small distilled model can be the right engineering call. Another is very different input or output modalities with tight hardware constraints, say something running on a phone. And sometimes there are product or safety reasons to isolate behavior.

But even then, the pattern I like is: train the big general model first, then derive the specialized ones from it, through distillation or fine-tuning. The general model is the source of truth, and the specialized models are deployment artifacts. If you go the other way and build specialists from scratch, you tend to get beaten a year later by the next general model that just does it better as a side effect.

r001.rationale: The response describes positive transfer but does not say anticipated negative transfer has generally failed to materialize.

r002.rationale: It gives practical reasons to split models, but does not identify measured negative transfer as one of them.

r003.rationale: It says capabilities reinforce each other and gives examples of coding, reasoning, math, and multilingual data helping across capabilities.

r004.rationale: It identifies latency and cost as reasons a narrow, high-volume task may warrant a smaller distilled model.

fable-5.1.text:
So my default bias, honestly, is toward the one big general model. I've spent a lot of my career watching specialized systems get eaten by general ones. People would build a very careful thing for one task, and then a bigger model trained on everything would just come along and do it better without anyone having tried. Transfer is real. The model learns things from code that help it with math, learns things from dialogue that help it with summarization. So if you split capabilities apart, you're usually giving up that shared knowledge, and you'd better be getting something concrete in return.

That said, there are a few reasons I'd split. One is cost and latency. If you have a capability that needs to run billions of times a day and the big model is overkill, then you want a small cheap thing. That's not really a question of what the model should know, it's a question of what you can afford to serve. Another is when the objective is genuinely different. If one use case wants the model to be fun and a bit unpredictable and another wants it to be very conservative and factual, you can push those apart with prompting and fine tuning for a while, but at some point the training signals are fighting each other and it's cleaner to have two things.

And then the interesting middle ground is mixture of experts, which is sort of my answer to "why choose." You let the model have a lot of specialized capacity internally, but you let gradient descent decide how to carve it up rather than a person deciding "this part is for French and this part is for chemistry." Humans are bad at drawing those boundaries. The model is pretty good at it. So you get most of the efficiency benefits of specialization while keeping the single model and the transfer.

The way I'd frame the decision is, don't split for reasons of taste or organizational convenience. Split when you can measure that the general model is paying a real tax on quality or cost for a specific use, and that tax won't go away with the next scale-up. Because a lot of the time it does go away, and then you've built two things where you only needed one.

r001.rationale: The response says specialized systems are often surpassed by larger general models and that transfer between capabilities is real, communicating that expected downsides of combining capabilities generally have not prevailed.

r002.rationale: It recommends splitting when a general model has a measurable quality tax for a specific use, and describes conflicting training signals as a reason to use separate models.

r003.rationale: It gives examples of positive transfer: code helping with math and dialogue helping with summarization, supporting shared capabilities in one model.

r004.rationale: It identifies serving cost and latency as reasons to use a smaller model when the general model is overkill for a frequent capability.

astra-6.text:
I think the default should be to share, because a lot of capabilities help each other. If you get better at understanding language, that helps you write code. If you get better at code, that may help you reason about other things. You don’t necessarily know in advance where that transfer is going to happen, so splitting everything up too early can lose something valuable.

But sharing a model doesn’t mean you have to use every parameter for every token. You can have a mixture of experts, where different parts of the network specialize, and the system learns which parts to use. That gives you a way to increase capacity without increasing computation proportionally.

Then there’s the practical question: if you have a narrow task that happens a billion times a day, can a much smaller model do it well enough? If so, that can be a very good reason to specialize. I’d look at the actual quality and cost tradeoff, rather than assume that the boundaries between models should match the categories humans use to describe tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says transfer can be hard to predict and that splitting too early can lose value, but does not state that anticipated negative transfer has generally failed to materialize.

r002.rationale: It gives no measured negative transfer between capabilities as a reason to separate them.

r003.rationale: It says capabilities can help one another, giving language understanding helping code and coding helping broader reasoning as reasons to share.

r004.rationale: It discusses quality and cost tradeoffs for a frequent narrow task, but does not clearly identify excessive serving cost as a limit on combining capabilities in one model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the default should be to share. If you train a model on a bunch of different tasks, sometimes they help each other in surprising ways. And you don’t necessarily know ahead of time which things are going to be useful for which other things.

But sharing knowledge doesn’t mean you have to activate the whole model for every token. That’s one of the appealing things about mixture of experts: you can have a lot of capacity, and use a relatively small amount of computation on each input. So you get some specialization inside a general model.

Ultimately, it’s an empirical question. Does training these things together improve quality? What does it cost to serve? If a specialized model does something substantially cheaper or better, that’s a good reason to have one. But I’d want to measure that advantage before giving up the benefits of sharing.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks can help each other, but does not say anticipated negative transfer generally failed to materialize.

r002.rationale: It gives a substantially cheaper or better specialized model as a reason to separate, but does not identify measured negative transfer as that reason.

r003.rationale: It says training different tasks together can help them in surprising ways, identifying positive transfer as a reason to share.

r004.rationale: It says serving cost should be evaluated and a substantially cheaper specialized model is a good reason to use one.
